nodes.description: Intravenous systemic administration of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector (serotype rh.10, cardiotropic) expressing the normal human frataxin (FXN) coding sequence. nodes.description: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting the FXN GAA-repeat-associated transcript or disease-causing splice mutations offer a strategy to raise endogenous FXN expression. Modified ASOs directed at the GAA repeat increase FXN protein more than threefold in patient cell lines, and ASOs correcting the c.165+5G>C splice-site mutation restore functional FXN transcript. Unlike gene addition, ASOs act on the endogenous transcript, potentially limiting the risk of FXN overexpression toxicity.

nodes.description: Investigational gene-editing strategies including CRISPR-Cas9 and zinc-finger nucleases (ZFN) targeting the GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene. Preclinical studies in patient-derived iPSCs demonstrate that GAA repeat removal restores FXN expression and ameliorates cellular phenotypes including improved mitochondrial function and neuronal survival. AAV-delivered CRISPR-Cas9 in mouse models achieves GAA repeat removal in heart, liver, and skeletal muscle, with successful FXN restoration in liver. These approaches offer potential advantages over gene addition by targeting the root genetic cause (the repeat expansion) rather than adding an extra FXN gene, and may reduce risk of FXN overexpression toxicity by restoring endogenous regulatory mechanisms.

nodes.description: An AAV-based gene therapy expressing the normal human FXN coding sequence, administered via dual routes: MRI-guided intradentate nucleus (IDN) infusion targeting cerebellar degeneration and systemic intravenous infusion targeting cardiac and skeletal muscle. Phase I FALCON trial (NCT07180355) initiated in 2026. Preclinical studies in mice show improved neurobehavioral and cardiac function with increased survival and ~33% reduction in LVMI. Non-human primate studies demonstrate successful dual-route FXN expression in both the dentate nucleus and heart, confirming feasibility of the surgical IDN injection approach in humans. Unlike LX2006 which targets cardiac tissue alone, SGT-212's dual-route design aims to address both neurological and cardiac manifestations of FRDA.
